oggetti/via-lattea/cosa: It's our galaxy, a barred spiral with hundreds of billions of stars. We're inside it, and the pale band across the sky is its disc seen edge-on.
oggetti/via-lattea/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from July to September, when the brightest part is high in the south after sunset.
oggetti/via-lattea/dove: You need a dark sky, away from lights: the band runs through Cygnus and Aquila and down to Sagittarius, where the centre lies. From the southern hemisphere the centre passes almost overhead and is far more spectacular.
oggetti/via-lattea/come: With the naked eye you see a long whitish cloud with dark patches; with binoculars it breaks up into thousands of stars.
oggetti/via-lattea/origine: The name comes from the Greek myth of the milk spilt by Hera while she was nursing Heracles. The word 'galaxy' also comes from the Greek 'gala', which means milk.
oggetti/via-lattea/storia: In 1610 Galileo, with his spyglass, discovered that the pale band is made of countless stars. In Italy it was also called the 'Strada di San Giacomo' (St James's Road), because pilgrims followed it towards Santiago de Compostela.
oggetti/m33/cosa: It's a spiral galaxy about 3 million light years away. It's the third-largest galaxy in our Local Group, after Andromeda and the Milky Way.
oggetti/m33/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from October to January.
oggetti/m33/dove: It lies between the star Alpha Trianguli and the star Mirach in Andromeda, on the opposite side of Mirach from the Andromeda Galaxy (M31). From the southern hemisphere it's low in the north.
oggetti/m33/come: With binoculars it's a large, very faint glow; in a town you can hardly see it.
oggetti/m33/origine: It takes its name from the small constellation Triangulum. M33 is number 33 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m33/storia: Charles Messier catalogued it in 1764. The Sicilian astronomer Giovanni Battista Hodierna may already have seen it before 1654.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/cosa: It's an irregular dwarf galaxy that orbits the Milky Way, about 160,000 light years away.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/quando: From the southern hemisphere it can be seen well all year round, but the best evenings are from November to March.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/dove: It can never be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere it's a large pale cloud in the southern sky, in the constellation Dorado, near the south celestial pole.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/come: To the naked eye it looks like a piece broken off the Milky Way; with binoculars you can see clusters and nebulae, such as the Tarantula Nebula.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/origine: It's named after Ferdinand Magellan, the navigator who led the first voyage around the world (1519-1522). Antonio Pigafetta, who was on board, described these clouds.
oggetti/grande-nube-magellano/storia: In 964 al-Sufi mentioned it under the name 'al-Bakr', the White Ox, visible from southern Arabia. The peoples of the southern hemisphere had always known it, and many Aboriginal Australian cultures have stories about these clouds.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/cosa: It's an irregular dwarf galaxy, a companion of the Milky Way, about 200,000 light years away.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/quando: From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from September to January.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/dove: It can never be seen from Italy. From the southern hemisphere it's in the constellation Tucana: look for it as a small pale cloud near the south celestial pole, next to the cluster 47 Tucanae.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/come: To the naked eye it's a small grey cloud; binoculars show a grainy patch.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/origine: Like its big sister, it's named after Ferdinand Magellan, because his voyage made the clouds known in Europe.
oggetti/piccola-nube-magellano/storia: European navigators also called them the 'Cape Clouds'. In 1912 Henrietta Leavitt studied its variable stars and discovered a method for measuring distances in the universe.
oggetti/m51/cosa: It's a spiral galaxy seen face-on, about 31 million light years away, with a small companion galaxy attached to one arm.
oggetti/m51/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from March to June, when it's high in the sky.
oggetti/m51/dove: Start from the star Alkaid, the last in the handle of the Plough, and move about 3.5 degrees south-west. From the southern hemisphere it's very low on the northern horizon.
oggetti/m51/come: With a small telescope you can see two small round smudges close together; the spiral arms need a very dark sky and a bigger telescope.
oggetti/m51/origine: The name 'Whirlpool' comes from its spiral shape. M51 is number 51 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m51/storia: Charles Messier discovered it in 1773. In 1845 Lord Rosse, with a large telescope in Ireland, drew its arms: it was the first galaxy in which a spiral shape was seen.
oggetti/m81/cosa: It's a large spiral galaxy about 12 million light years away.
oggetti/m81/quando: From Italy it's visible all year round because it's close to the north pole, but the best evenings are from January to May.
oggetti/m81/dove: Draw a line from the star Phecda to the star Dubhe in the Plough and extend it by about the same length. It can't be seen from the southern hemisphere.
oggetti/m81/come: With binoculars it's a small grey oval smudge, with the fainter M82 beside it.
oggetti/m81/origine: It's named after Johann Elert Bode, the German astronomer who discovered it. M81 is number 81 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m81/storia: Bode discovered it on 31 December 1774, together with M82. Messier added it to his catalogue in 1781.
oggetti/m82/cosa: It's a galaxy seen edge-on, about 12 million light years away, where stars are being born at a very fast rate.
oggetti/m82/quando: From Italy it's visible all year round, but the best evenings are from January to May.
oggetti/m82/dove: It lies half a degree north of M81, in the same binocular field. It can't be seen from the southern hemisphere.
oggetti/m82/come: With binoculars it's a thin, faint dash next to M81; a small telescope shows its elongated shape.
oggetti/m82/origine: The name 'Cigar' comes from its long, narrow shape. M82 is number 82 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m82/storia: Johann Elert Bode discovered it in 1774 together with M81. Its disturbed shape is due to a close encounter with M81.
oggetti/m104/cosa: It's a spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on, about 28 million light years away, with a very bright central bulge.
oggetti/m104/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from April to June.
oggetti/m104/dove: It's in Virgo, near the border with Corvus: start from the four-sided shape of Corvus and extend towards the north-east. From the southern hemisphere it's high in the sky.
oggetti/m104/come: With a small telescope it's a bright oval; the thin dark lane of dust can only be seen with bigger instruments.
oggetti/m104/origine: The name comes from the Mexican hat, the sombrero, because the galaxy looks like one. M104 is number 104 in Messier's list.
oggetti/m104/storia: Pierre Méchain discovered it in 1781. It wasn't in Messier's printed catalogue: it was only added as M104 in 1921.
oggetti/ngc-253/cosa: It's a spiral galaxy seen almost edge-on, about 11 million light years away, where a great many stars are being born.
oggetti/ngc-253/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from October to December, but it always stays low in the south.
oggetti/ngc-253/dove: Start from the star Diphda (Beta Ceti) and go down about 7 degrees towards the south. From the southern hemisphere it passes almost overhead and is much easier.
oggetti/ngc-253/come: With binoculars it's an elongated grey spindle, surprisingly large if the southern horizon is clear.
oggetti/ngc-253/origine: It takes its name from the constellation Sculptor. NGC 253 is number 253 in the New General Catalogue, published in 1888.
oggetti/ngc-253/storia: Caroline Herschel discovered it in 1783, while she was looking for comets. It's also called the 'Silver Coin Galaxy' because of its appearance.
oggetti/ngc-5128/cosa: It's a giant elliptical galaxy crossed by a band of dust, more than 10 million light years away. It has a very active central black hole.
oggetti/ngc-5128/quando: From the southern hemisphere the best evenings are from April to July. From Italy it can only be seen from the south, skimming the horizon, in May.
oggetti/ngc-5128/dove: It lies about 4 degrees north of the cluster Omega Centauri, in the constellation Centaurus. From the southern hemisphere it's high in the sky.
oggetti/ngc-5128/come: With binoculars it's a small round smudge; a small telescope shows the dark band that divides it.
oggetti/ngc-5128/origine: The name comes from the constellation Centaurus; the 'A' shows that it's the strongest source of radio waves in that constellation. NGC 5128 is its number in the New General Catalogue.
oggetti/ngc-5128/storia: James Dunlop discovered it in 1826, from Australia. In the mid-20th century it was realised that it's one of the most powerful radio sources in the sky.
oggetti/m101/cosa: It's a large spiral galaxy seen face-on, about 21 million light years away, much larger than the Milky Way.
oggetti/m101/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from April to July.
oggetti/m101/dove: It forms a triangle with the stars Mizar and Alkaid, in the handle of the Plough. From the southern hemisphere it stays just above the northern horizon and is almost impossible to see.
oggetti/m101/come: With a small telescope it's a large, very faint glow, hard to see if the sky isn't dark.
oggetti/m101/origine: The name 'Pinwheel' comes from its wide-open spiral arms. M101 is number 101 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m101/storia: Pierre Méchain discovered it in 1781 and Messier added it to his catalogue. In 2011 a supernova exploded in it that could be seen with small telescopes.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/cosa: Three spiral galaxies close to one another, more than 30 million light years away.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from March to May.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/dove: They lie halfway between the stars Chertan (Theta Leonis) and Iota Leonis, below the Lion's hindquarters. From the southern hemisphere you see them in the north, with Leo upside down.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/come: With a small telescope you can see three small grey smudges in the same field; NGC 3628 is the faintest.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/origine: The name comes from the constellation Leo. M65 and M66 are in Messier's catalogue, NGC 3628 in the New General Catalogue.
oggetti/tripletto-leone/storia: Pierre Méchain discovered M65 and M66 in 1780. William Herschel found the third, NGC 3628, in 1784.
oggetti/m77/cosa: It's a spiral galaxy with a very active nucleus, about 47 million light years away.
oggetti/m77/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from October to January.
oggetti/m77/dove: It lies about 1 degree from the star Delta Ceti, in the constellation Cetus. From the southern hemisphere it's halfway up in the north.
oggetti/m77/come: With a small telescope it looks almost like a blurry star, because of its very bright nucleus.
oggetti/m77/origine: It's in the constellation Cetus (the Whale), the sea monster in the myth of Andromeda. M77 is number 77 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m77/storia: Pierre Méchain discovered it in 1780; Messier thought it was a star cluster with nebulosity. Today it's the model for 'Seyfert galaxies', with an active central black hole.
oggetti/m83/cosa: It's a barred spiral galaxy seen face-on, about 15 million light years away.
oggetti/m83/quando: The best evenings from Italy are from April to June, but it stays low in the south.
oggetti/m83/dove: It's in Hydra, on the border with Centaurus: start from Spica and go down about 20 degrees towards the south. From the southern hemisphere it passes high in the sky.
oggetti/m83/come: With binoculars it's a small round smudge; a small telescope shows the bright nucleus.
oggetti/m83/origine: The name 'Southern Pinwheel' comes from its spiral shape and its position in the southern sky. M83 is number 83 in Messier's catalogue.
oggetti/m83/storia: Nicolas-Louis de Lacaille discovered it in 1752, from the Cape of Good Hope in South Africa. Messier added it to his catalogue in 1781.
